You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: Can MVFA's few-shot patch memory bank — which stores every patch feature of the K support images at four feature levels, grows linearly with K and resolution, and retains raw patient-derived features — be replaced by a small set of M learned normal prototypes per feature level (M much smaller than K times the number of patches) fitted only on the K normal support images, such that few-shot anomaly classification and segmentation AUROC on BMAD is preserved while memory is reduced by at least an order of magnitude and no raw patch features are stored? The study should quantify the accuracy-versus-M trade-off, the memory and retrieval-time savings, and whether prototype distances model the compact normal distribution better than nearest-neighbour distances to individual patches.
Rationale: Limitations G7 and G13 point at the same design decision: MVFA's few-shot comparison branch assumes nothing about the structure of normality and simply memorises all normal patches, which is costly, privacy-sensitive, and does not exploit the fact that normal tissue occupies a compact region of feature space while anomalies are diverse. Related work shows the alternatives are emerging but not in MVFA's multi-level medical setting: MadCLIP removes the memory bank altogether by using dual normal/abnormal adapter branches with a SigLIP loss, APRIL-GAN and MVFA keep per-level memory banks, and the intrinsic-normal-prototype line of work in universal anomaly detection extracts prototypes from a single image rather than learning a compact normal model per modality. A per-level prototype memory is a fine-grained change to one component — the few-shot branch — and can be implemented as k-means or learnable prototypes on the frozen adapted features from the public MVFA code, evaluated with one GPU. Because the prototypes summarise the support set, the privacy question can be addressed concretely by measuring whether any stored vector is close to an individual training patch. The modality-disjoint and multi-draw protocol is especially important here, since prototype quality depends on which K support images are drawn.

Feedback: Specify how prototypes are fitted (k-means versus learned) and which M values are tested.
- Relevance: rating 4/5. Review: Relevant to G7 and G13 and to the few-shot branch of MVFA; related to APRIL-GAN and MadCLIP's memory-free design. Feedback: Explain why compressing a few-shot memory bank matters in MVFA's regime.
- Originality: rating 2/5. Review: Memory-bank compression is established: PatchCore's coreset subsampling and prototype-based normality models (including intrinsic normal prototype methods) already address exactly this. Applying k-means prototypes to MVFA's adapted features is a minor variation. Feedback: Find an angle that existing compression methods do not cover, for example prototypes shared across modalities, or prototypes learned jointly with the adapters.
- Feasibility: rating 5/5. Review: Straightforward to implement and evaluate on BMAD with one GPU. Feedback: None.
- Significance: rating 2/5. Review: The motivation is weak in MVFA's actual regime: with K between 2 and 16 support images at 240x240 resolution, the memory bank holds only a few thousand vectors per level, so memory and retrieval cost are not a practical bottleneck. The privacy argument is also limited, because centroids of a handful of images can still be close to individual patches. Gains are therefore likely to be small. Feedback: Either move to a regime where memory matters (larger K, higher resolution, 3D volumes) or reframe the problem around modelling the compactness of normality, which is the more significant question in G7.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G5. Prompting is static, generic, and domain-agnostic: The text encoder is kept frozen, and the prompts consist of hand-crafted normal/abnormal state descriptions averaged over 35 ImageNet templates. This design presumes a single, universal visual-language concept of “normal” and “abnormal” that holds uniformly across imaging modalities, and it omits instance-adaptive, visually conditioned, or hybrid prompting strategies. No prompt-sensitivity analysis is provided.
- G7. Normal/anomaly disentanglement and distributional asymmetry are not made explicit: The dual- adapter design separates anomaly-classification and anomaly-segmentation features, but it does not explicitly model the compact distribution of normal samples against the comparatively diverse distribution of abnormal samples. The method relies on shared adapted features and a few-shot normal memory bank without routing mechanisms, dual normal/abnormal pathways, or many-to- one, SigLIP-style regularization.
- G13. Scalability, memory, and privacy considerations are unaddressed: The method uses a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone and trains six separate leave-one-out models for 50 epochs each on a single RTX 3090 GPU; training and inference time, memory footprint, and parameter counts are not reported. The term “lightweight” refers only to the adapters, not to the overall system. The few-shot memory bank grows with K and with spatial resolution, yet retrieval cost and the privacy and governance implications of storing patient-derived features are not analyzed. Downscaling to a 240 × 240 resolution and processing volumetric data as 2D slices may cause small lesions and broader 3D CT/MRI context to be lost.

Problem: Does explicitly modelling normality as compact improve MVFA's zero-shot transfer to unseen modalities? MVFA aligns patches symmetrically to one 'normal' and one 'abnormal' text anchor and stores raw support patches for few-shot comparison, so nothing in its objective encodes that normal tissue is compact while anomalies are diverse. We ask whether adding, at each of the four adapter levels, a set of M learnable normal prototypes trained jointly with the adapters on the source modalities — with a compactness loss pulling normal patches to their nearest prototype and a margin loss pushing abnormal patches away — improves zero-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on the held-out modality, and whether the learned prototypes, re-estimated from K normal target images, can replace the patch memory bank in the few-shot setting without loss of accuracy. Outcomes are reported for M in {8, 32, 128}, under the modality-disjoint, 3-seed protocol.

Rationale: The reviewers judged memory compression in the few-shot regime insignificant because the bank is small, and pointed to the more important question in G7 — modelling the compactness of normality. The problem is reframed accordingly: prototypes are learned jointly with the adapters on source data (not fitted post hoc as in PatchCore coresets), which is the element existing compression methods do not cover, and the few-shot replacement becomes a secondary outcome rather than the motivation. It is a contained change to the training objective in the public MVFA code and feasible on one GPU.
